name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPR-47 'Ancestor'
description:
The KPR-47 is Kang-Petrov's unabashed acknowledgment of what it is and where it came from. Chambered in 7.62mm Soviet Pattern, the KPR-47 runs on a long-stroke piston system descended in near-unbroken lineage from a design that predates the megacity by two centuries. Stamped steel receiver, chrome-lined barrel, rotating bolt with dual locking lugs — every component is manufactured to tolerances that prioritize function over precision. The rifle will cycle dirty, wet, partially obstructed, and half-assembled by someone who learned to use it from a video tutorial. Effective range sits around 350 meters, though the 7.62mm Soviet Pattern round carries authority well past that. Standard magazine is 30 rounds, and it will accept aftermarket polymer double-stacks and the older steel banana mags that have been floating around GLMZ for decades. Weight runs 3.8 kilograms empty, which is honest weight — you feel it, but you trust it.

The KPR-47 is what shelf workers save three months of wages to buy, and what some of them never have to — because their parents already have one in a closet, wrapped in a cloth that smells like machine oil and old decisions. Kang-Petrov sells it in blued steel and in a matte polymer furniture variant they call the 'Civic Package,' which is exactly as condescending as it sounds. The rifle is legal under standard registration in most GLMZ districts, which means Arcturus Civil Security technically can't confiscate it unless they have cause — and they will find cause if they want to. Tier 1 buyers get the rifle. What they do with it is the conversation that makes Tier 4 nervous.

Every KPR-47 that has been in GLMZ longer than five years looks like it has been in GLMZ longer than five years. The bluing wears off the high-contact points first — the pistol grip, the charging handle, the front sight post — leaving bare steel that oxidizes to a gray-brown that is not quite rust but is heading there. Owners fill these spots with marker, with nail polish, with a smear of grease that never quite dries. The rifles accumulate stickers, scratches, and the occasional notch that someone put there deliberately and someone else inherited without knowing why. There is a KPR-47 currently in the possession of a woman in the Bridgeport Exclusion Ring whose serial number traces back to a Slagworks factory stamp from 2031. The steel is not the same steel. The springs have been replaced four times. The barrel is third-generation. But the receiver is original, and she will tell you that means the rifle is original, and she is not wrong.
specifications:
caliber: 7.62mm Soviet Pattern
effective_range: 350m
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic / Full-automatic
magazine_capacity: 30 rounds
weight: 3.8 kg
tactical_use: The KPR-47 is a volume weapon and a presence weapon. Operators run it at short-to-medium range where the 7.62mm Soviet Pattern round does the work that intimidation started. Full-auto is largely ceremonial past 100 meters — experienced users keep it on semi and let the caliber carry the argument. In GLMZ's corridor environments, parking structures, and collapsed-floor tenements, the rifle's compactness relative to its power makes it the go-to for anyone who needs to be taken seriously without spending Φ they don't have on optics and accessories. Most operators run iron sights because iron sights don't need charging.
cultural_context: The KPR-47 is generational in a way that makes Arcturus Civil Security uncomfortable. It is the rifle that shows up in exclusion zone standoffs, in the Gray Zone district mutual aid caches, in the back of every Excluded community that has decided to stop dying quietly. Corponation security forces call it 'legacy hardware' in briefings, which is their way of saying they have been dealing with this rifle for longer than their grandparents have been alive and it has not gotten easier. Owning a KPR-47 in a Tier 1 district is a statement. It is not always a loud statement. Sometimes it is the quietest possible statement, which is worse.
story_hooks: A KPR-47 recovered from an Excluded zone standoff has a serial number that Arcturus Civil Security flagged as destroyed in a 2187 confiscation sweep — someone in the property destruction division has been running a resale operation for forty years, and the rifle just became evidence.
Kyle Corbin-Vasik's contact hands him a KPR-47 wrapped in the same oilcloth his father used to keep his own rifle in — the serial numbers don't match, but the scratches on the pistol grip do.
